# Sign Language Translator — llms.txt

> Free learning aid that converts English text into American Sign Language
> or British Sign Language sign sequences. Built and maintained by Firoz Khan
> of FK Digital Media.

## What this site does

- Text-to-sign translator with an ASL/BSL toggle: type English text and step
  through it sign by sign. Whole words and phrases are matched against the
  selected language's dictionary first; unmatched words are fingerspelled
  letter by letter (ASL: one-handed A–Z, 0–9; BSL: two-handed A–Z).
- ASL signs dictionary (57 signs) and BSL signs dictionary (47 signs): common
  words and phrases with step-by-step, text-based sign descriptions and
  practice tips. Searchable, filterable by category. Each language was
  researched independently — BSL is a separate language from ASL, not a
  dialect, and signs are never swapped between languages.
- ASL alphabet & numbers reference: A–Z handshapes (J and Z are motion
  letters) and numbers 0–10.
- BSL alphabet & numbers reference: two-handed A–Z handshapes (H and J use a
  small movement) and numbers 1–5.

## Honest limitations (stated on the site itself)

- ASL and BSL each have their own grammar — word order differs from English.
  The translator shows vocabulary sign by sign; it does not rearrange
  sentences into either language's grammar.
- This is a learning aid, not a substitute for a qualified interpreter.
  For medical, legal, or emergency communication, use a certified interpreter.
- Sign descriptions are text-based step-by-step guides researched from
  established references (ASL: Lifeprint, university and public-health
  materials; BSL: BSL SignBank, BDA-adjacent teaching materials, BSL
  dictionaries) and rewritten in original words. Signer-created photos and
  videos are a planned future upgrade. No AI-generated hand images are used.
- BSL coverage is growing: words without a researched BSL sign are
  fingerspelled with an honest "not yet researched" note, never substituted
  with the ASL sign.

## Learning articles

- [I Miss You in Sign Language: How to Sign It in ASL & BSL](https://signlanguage-translator.com/blog/i-miss-you-in-sign-language/) (2026-10-06): Learn to sign ‘I miss you’ in American Sign Language: the I-MISS-YOU construction step by step, what to do in BSL, and common mistakes to avoid.
- [How to Fingerspell Your Name in ASL: A Step-by-Step Practice Guide](https://signlanguage-translator.com/learn/how-to-fingerspell-your-name-in-asl/) (2026-10-07): Learn to spell your name with the one-handed ASL alphabet: letter-by-letter steps, the J and Z motion letters, and practice tips for smooth, readable fingerspelling.
- [How to Fingerspell Your Name in BSL](https://signlanguage-translator.com/learn/how-to-fingerspell-your-name-in-bsl/) (2026-10-08): Spell your name with the two-handed BSL alphabet: how the base hand works, the vowel positions, the H and J movements, and practice tips for clear fingerspelling.
- [ASL vs BSL: 7 Key Differences Every Beginner Should Know](https://signlanguage-translator.com/learn/asl-vs-bsl-key-differences/) (2026-10-09): American and British Sign Language are separate languages, not dialects. The seven differences that matter most: alphabets, vocabulary, grammar, numbers, mouthing, fingerspelling use, and learning paths.
